title: The Great Seljuk Empire
subtitle: 1037–1194 · Tughril to Sanjar: Turkmen Conquest, the Sunni Sultanate at Baghdad, the Nizamiyya, the Assassins and the Collapse after Qatwan

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Tughril and Chaghri, Alp Arslan, Malik-Shah and Nizam al-Mulk, the succession wars and Sanjar

entries.label: Tughril Beg and Chaghri Beg
entries.hint: Tughril and Chaghri, grandsons of the chieftain Seljuk of the Oghuz, took Nishapur in 1038 and, after the victory of Dandanqan over the Ghaznavids in 1040, divided the east between them, Tughril ruling in the west; he entered Baghdad in December 1055, was invested as sultan by the Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im, took the title King of the East and West and married the caliph's daughter in 1063, the first Turkish ruler of the central Islamic lands.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; Bayhaqi, Tarikh-i Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Cambridge History of Iran vol. 5 (1968); Carole Hillenbrand, Turkish Myth and Muslim Symbol (2007).

entries.label: Alp Arslan
entries.hint: Alp Arslan, Tughril's nephew and successor, put down the rebellion of his cousin Qutalmish, took Armenia and Georgia, defeated Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert in August 1071 and was killed by a captive fortress commander in November 1072 on an expedition to Transoxiana; his reign, with Nizam al-Mulk as vizier, established the Seljuk administration.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Hillenbrand 2007; Bosworth 1968.

entries.label: Malik-Shah I
entries.hint: Malik-Shah, who came to the throne aged seventeen, extended the empire from the Oxus and Kashgar to the Mediterranean and Yemen, with Isfahan as his capital and Baghdad as a second seat, held the pilgrimage roads and the Hijaz and brought a period of order that later Persian writers made the golden age of the Seljuks; he died in November 1092, a month after the murder of his vizier.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Rawandi, Rahat al-sudur; Bosworth 1968; Ann Lambton, Continuity and Change in Medieval Persia (1988).

entries.label: Sanjar
entries.hint: Ahmad Sanjar, governor of Khurasan from 1097, became the senior sultan in 1118 and ruled from Merv a realm that stretched from Transoxiana to Iraq, a ruler remembered for his wars against the Ghaznavids and Qarakhanids and the Khwarazmshahs; he lost the battle of Qatwan to the Kara-Khitai in 1141, was captured by the Ghuzz in 1153 and died in 1157, leaving no heir and the empire divided.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; Bosworth 1968; Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017).

entries.label: Nizam al-Mulk
entries.hint: Nizam al-Mulk (Abu Ali al-Hasan al-Tusi), vizier of Alp Arslan and Malik-Shah for thirty years, ran the empire's government, with a network of couriers and inspectors, set up the Nizamiyya madrasas, wrote the Siyasatnama, a book of government, and filled the administration with his sons and clients; he was killed by an Assassin disguised as a Sufi on 14 October 1092 on the road to Baghdad.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama (trans. Darke, 1960); Ibn al-Athir; Lambton 1988; Neguin Yavari, The Future of the Past in Persian Historiography (2014).
keywords: Nizam al-Mulk Abu Ali al-Hasan al-Tusi

entries.label: The Seljuk offshoots: Kirman, Syria and Rum
entries.hint: Qavurd's dynasty ruled Kirman from 1041 to 1186; Tutush, Malik-Shah's brother, founded in 1078 the Seljuk line in Syria and the rulers of Damascus and Aleppo, ending with his sons' fall to the atabegs in 1117, and Suleyman ibn Qutalmish and his successors, the sultans of Rum, held on in Anatolia until the Mongol conquest, the longest-lived of the branches.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, The Islamic Dynasties (1967); Hillenbrand 1999.

entries.label: The wars of the succession
entries.hint: After Malik-Shah's death his widow Terken Khatun tried to put her young son Mahmud on the throne, and the sons of the sultan, Barkyaruq, Muhammad and Sanjar, fought for twenty-five years, with the dissolution of the empire into a set of principalities of Kirman, Syria, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Khurasan under the sultan's relatives and the atabegs; Barkyaruq's rule (1092–1105) was a period of coups and paid soldiers.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth 1968; Hillenbrand, The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives (1999).

entries.label: The sultans of Iraq and the end
entries.hint: The Seljuk sultans of Iraq and western Iran, Muhammad II, Sulayman-Shah, Arslan-Shah and Tughril III, ruled from Hamadan, dominated by the atabegs of Azerbaijan, the Ildegizids, and by the caliph al-Nasir who sought to restore Abbasid independence; Tughril III was defeated and killed by the Khwarazmshah Tekish near Rayy in March 1194, ending the sultanate in Iran.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani; Bosworth 1968; Jackson 2017.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Dandanqan, Baghdad, Manzikert, Alamut, the conquest of Syria, Qatwan, the Ghuzz and the end at Rayy

entries.label: The battle of Dandanqan
entries.hint: At the desert fort of Dandanqan the Seljuk Turkmen cavalry, which had refused to join the Ghaznavid slave army in plain battle, wore down Masud I's heavy army with hit-and-run harassment and defeated it; Masud fled to India and was murdered, and the Ghaznavids lost Khurasan and became an Indian state with Lahore and Ghazna as its capitals.
entries.note: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids (1963).

entries.label: The entry into Baghdad
entries.hint: Invited by the Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im to relieve him of the Shia Buyid emirs and the Turkish general al-Basasiri, Tughril entered Baghdad on 18 December 1055, was received with honours and installed as the caliph's protector; the Buyids' end ushered in a period of Sunni Turkish rule at the heart of the Abbasid caliphate.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Bosworth 1968; Hillenbrand 2007.

entries.label: The Seljuk conquest of Syria and Palestine
entries.hint: The Turkmen commander Atsiz ibn Uwaq took Ramla and Jerusalem from the Fatimids in 1071–1073 and Damascus in 1076, was killed by Tutush in 1079 and Tutush ruled Syria; Seljuk and Turkmen rule broke the Fatimid hold on Palestine, Jerusalem's Christian pilgrims were affected, and a Turkish military society replaced an Arab, Shia order in much of Syria, which the crusaders met in 1097–1099.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Qalanisi, Dhayl; Hillenbrand 1999; Thierry Bianquis, Damas et la Syrie sous la domination fatimide (1986).

entries.label: Manzikert
entries.hint: Alp Arslan, on his way to deal with the Fatimids in Syria, met the army of Romanos IV Diogenes near Lake Van, and with a force perhaps a third the size defeated and captured the emperor, whom he released on terms; the victory itself was of limited immediate effect, but the Byzantine civil wars that followed opened Anatolia to Turkmen settlement, and the date is the conventional start of Turkish Anatolia.
entries.note: Attaleiates; Ibn al-Athir; Hillenbrand 2007; Alexander Beihammer, Byzantium and the Emergence of Muslim-Turkish Anatolia (2017).

entries.label: Hasan-i Sabbah and the capture of Alamut
entries.hint: Hasan-i Sabbah, a Persian Ismaili missionary who had spent years in Cairo and then led the Nizari Ismaili movement, took the mountain fortress of Alamut in the Elburz by a ruse in 1090 and made it the base of a network of strongholds across Iran and Syria, with a policy of assassination of leading figures as the weapon of the weak against the Seljuk military; the sultans' attempts to storm the castles failed.
entries.note: Juvayni, History of the World Conqueror (trans. Boyle, 1958); Rashid al-Din; Farhad Daftary, The Ismāʿīlīs (1990); Bernard Lewis, The Assassins (1967).

entries.label: The killing of Nizam al-Mulk
entries.hint: The vizier, being carried in his litter near Nihavand on the way from Isfahan to Baghdad, was stabbed by a youth disguised as a Sufi, a Nizari Ismaili from Daylam; Malik-Shah died thirty-five days later, and the murder, a model for many later killings of emirs, qadis and viziers, set the Assassins' fame; the Seljuk historians attributed it also to court rivalry.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Rawandi; Daftary 1990; Lewis 1967.

entries.label: The First Crusade and the Seljuk response
entries.hint: The crusader armies met divided Turkish powers: the Rum sultan Kilij Arslan I was beaten at Nicaea and Dorylaion in 1097, the Seljuk atabeg Kerbogha of Mosul failed to relieve Antioch in June 1098, and Jerusalem, held by the Fatimids since 1098, was taken by the Franks on 15 July 1099; the Great Seljuk sultans, busy with civil war, sent no army.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Qalanisi; Hillenbrand 1999; Christopher Tyerman, God's War (2006).

entries.label: Qatwan
entries.hint: When the Qarakhanid ruler appealed for help against the Qarluq and Kangli, Sanjar marched to Samarkand and fought the Kara-Khitai, a Buddhist Khitan people from northern China under the gurkhan Yelü Dashi, on the Qatwan steppe; his army was destroyed and his wife captured, and the Khitans took Transoxiana, an event that fed the later legend of Prester John in Europe.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani; Michal Biran, The Empire of the Qara Khitai in Eurasian History (2005); Jackson 2017.

entries.label: The Ghuzz revolt and the sack of Khurasan
entries.hint: When the Ghuzz Turkmen of Khurasan, who had been put under heavy dues, rebelled in 1153, they defeated Sanjar's army near Balkh, captured him and kept him in captivity for three years, sacked Merv, Nishapur, Tus and Sabzavar and massacred the population and the scholars of Nishapur; Sanjar escaped in 1156 and died in 1157, and the realm disappeared.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani; Rawandi; Bosworth 1968.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The iqta and the atabeg, the sultan and the caliph, the Nizamiyya system and the vizier's book

entries.label: Sultan and caliph
entries.hint: The Seljuk sultan was invested by the caliph with the symbols of authority, a robe, a diploma and the title of Sultan, in a ceremony at which the caliph's name was read first in the Friday sermon and the coins, as a Sunni layer of legitimacy to a rule that rested on the army; the caliph kept spiritual authority and a small territory in Iraq, the sultan the government of the world.
entries.note: Al-Mawardi, al-Ahkam al-sultaniyya; Bosworth 1968; Lambton 1988.

entries.label: The iqta
entries.hint: The Seljuk system paid the army's emirs and soldiers by iqta, the assignment of the tax revenue of a district for life or a term, without ownership of the land, as set out by Nizam al-Mulk in the Siyasatnama, who warned that the holders should not oppress the peasants; in practice, with the unrest after 1092, iqtas became hereditary and led to a fragmented military aristocracy.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama 13; Ann Lambton, ‘Reflections on the Iqta’ (1962); Lambton 1988.

entries.label: The Nizamiyya madrasas
entries.hint: Nizam al-Mulk founded between 1064 and 1092 a system of colleges for Shafi'i law and Ashari theology in Baghdad (opened in 1067), Nishapur, Isfahan, Basra, Mosul, Herat and other towns, with endowments and salaries for teachers and stipends for students, to train the officials and judges of a Sunni state and to counter Ismaili doctrine; teachers included al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; George Makdisi, The Rise of Colleges (1981); Lambton 1988.

entries.label: The atabegs
entries.hint: The atabeg, a Turkish commander appointed as tutor and guardian of a young Seljuk prince, became in the twelfth century the effective ruler of his charge's province and founded dynasties, among them the Zangids of Mosul and Aleppo, the Ildegizids of Azerbaijan and the Salghurids of Fars; the atabeg states were the power on the Muslim side in the crusader wars.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth 1967; Hillenbrand 1999.

entries.label: The Siyasatnama
entries.hint: At the sultan's request in 1091 Nizam al-Mulk set down in fifty chapters his advice on the government of a kingdom: justice, the army, the spies, the treatment of non-Muslims and of Ismailis, whom he accused of subversion; the book is the best-known of the Mirrors for Princes and a source for the ideals of Seljuk rule, although its last chapters on heretics were probably added after his death.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama (trans. Hubert Darke, 1960); Lambton 1988; Yavari 2014.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Sunni revival, the Assassins, al-Ghazali and the Sufi shaykhs

entries.label: Abu Said and the Sufi shaykhs of Khurasan
entries.hint: Abu Said Abu'l-Khayr (967–1049), the Sufi of Mayhana, and Abu'l-Hasan Kharaqani, Abdullah Ansari of Herat (d. 1089), who wrote prayers and the Munajat in Persian, Qushayri (d. 1072) with his treatise, and Ahmad Yasavi (d. 1166) in Turkestan were the founders of the Sufi tradition in Persian and Turkic, with khanqahs patronised by the Seljuk emirs and viziers.
entries.note: Qushayri, Risala; Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-tawhid (trans. John O'Kane, 1992); Fritz Meier, Abu Saʿid-i Abu l-Hayr (1976).

entries.label: The Sunni restoration
entries.hint: The Seljuks, Hanafi Turks who regarded themselves as champions of Sunni orthodoxy against the Shia Buyids and the Fatimid anti-caliphs, made a policy of Sunni revival with support for the madrasas, the cursing of heretics, the end of the public Shia ritual in Baghdad and the encouragement of Ashari theology and Shafi'i law; the Ash'ari preachers' persecution at the start of Tughril's reign, the Fitna of 1060s, shows the conflicts.
entries.note: Makdisi 1981; Daniella Talmon-Heller, Islamic Piety in Medieval Syria (2007); Bosworth 1968.

entries.label: Al-Ghazali
entries.hint: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, a Shafi'i jurist and theologian of Tus, the professor of the Nizamiyya at Baghdad from 1091, wrote the Tahafut al-falasifa against the philosophers, the Munqidh min al-dalal on his spiritual crisis in 1095 and years as a Sufi wanderer, and the Ihya ulum al-din, the revival of the religious sciences, which joined the law with mysticism and became the most influential work of Sunni Islam after the Quran and hadith.
entries.note: Al-Ghazali, Tahafut al-falasifa; al-Munqidh min al-dalal; Ihya ulum al-din; Michael Marmura (ed.); Frank Griffel, Al-Ghazali's Philosophical Theology (2009).

entries.label: The Nizari Ismailis and the Fatimid split
entries.hint: The succession dispute after the death of the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir in 1094 divided the Ismailis into followers of the elder son Nizar, who was passed over, and the new caliph al-Musta'li; Hasan-i Sabbah and his mountain network supported Nizar's line, the Nizaris, who formed an independent state of castles, and their Syrian branch, headed by Rashid al-Din Sinan (d. 1193), was the Assassins of the crusader chronicles.
entries.note: Daftary 1990; Rashid al-Din; Juvayni.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The domes of Isfahan, the Sanjar mausoleum, Persian and Arabic literature of the age

entries.label: The Persian prose and poetry of the age
entries.hint: The Persian language became that of the Seljuk court: Nasir Khusraw's Safarnama (1045–1052), an Ismaili poet's account of travel from Balkh to Cairo and Mecca; Gurgani's Vis o Ramin; Anvari and Sana'i's Hadiqat al-haqiqa (c. 1130) in the verse of religious mysticism; the Chahar maqala of Nizami Aruzi (c. 1155) and the Arabic Maqamat of al-Hariri of Basra (c. 1100), all show the literary world of the sultans.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, Safarnama; Hariri, Maqamat; Nizami Aruzi, Chahar maqala; Julie Scott Meisami, Medieval Persian Court Poetry (1987).
keywords: Arabic Maqamat of al-Hariri of Basra

entries.label: Omar Khayyam's quatrains
entries.hint: Omar Khayyam (1048–1131), an astronomer, mathematician and philosopher of Nishapur, is credited with several hundred Persian quatrains (rubaiyat) of doubt and enjoyment of the moment, which were first assembled in the thirteenth century and, in Edward FitzGerald's free version of 1859, made him one of the best-known Persian names in the West; which are authentic is disputed.
entries.note: Omar Khayyam, Rubaiyat; Ali Dashti, In Search of Omar Khayyam (1971); Edward FitzGerald, Rubáiyát (1859).

entries.label: The domes of the Friday Mosque of Isfahan
entries.hint: The south dome, built by Nizam al-Mulk about 1086–1087, and the north dome, built by his rival Taj al-Mulk in 1088–1089, above the old congregational mosque of Isfahan, with their squinches, brick ribs and inscriptions, are among the finest domed chambers in Islam and the models of Persian architecture of the next century.
entries.note: Robert Hillenbrand, Islamic Architecture (1994); Oleg Grabar, The Great Mosque of Isfahan (1990); Arthur Upham Pope, Persian Architecture (1965).

entries.label: The mausoleum of Sanjar at Merv
entries.hint: The mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar at Merv, a square building about 27 metres on each side and 38 metres high, with a double dome of which the outer was blue-tiled and a gallery around its drum, was built in his lifetime, probably about 1152–1157, and was, in the twelfth century, the largest mausoleum of the Islamic world.
entries.note: Hillenbrand 1994; Georgina Herrmann, The Monuments of Merv (1999).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Omar Khayyam and the calendar, al-Ghazali, Nasir Khusraw and the Siyasatnama

entries.label: Nasir Khusraw and Ismaili thought
entries.hint: Nasir Khusraw, a poet and philosopher from Balkh who became a Fatimid missionary after a pilgrimage in 1046–1052 and spent his last decades in exile in the mountains of Badakhshan, wrote the Safarnama and the Jami al-hikmatayn, a synthesis of philosophy and revelation in the Ismaili tradition; his followers still keep his memory among the Ismailis of Central Asia.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw, Safarnama and Jami al-hikmatayn; Alice Hunsberger, Nasir Khusraw (2000).

entries.label: Al-Juwayni and the theory of the imamate
entries.hint: Abu al-Maali al-Juwayni, Imam al-Haramayn, teacher of al-Ghazali, wrote Ghiyath al-umam on the imamate and the case of its absence, in which he argued that the community's duty was to its law and, where the caliph could not fulfil his office, to an effective ruler and the scholars; the argument, with the work of Mawardi, was a basis for the sultanate's legal acceptance.
entries.note: Juwayni, Ghiyath al-umam; Patricia Crone, Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004); Hillenbrand.

entries.label: Omar Khayyam's algebra
entries.hint: In his Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra Khayyam gave a geometrical solution of cubic equations by the intersection of conic sections, with a classification of the cases, and in the Commentary on the Difficulties of the Postulates of Euclid's Book he took up the parallel postulate; he was the greatest mathematician of his day.
entries.note: Khayyam, Risala fi'l-barahin ala masa'il al-jabr wa'l-muqabala; Roshdi Rashed and Bijan Vahabzadeh, Omar Khayyam the Mathematician (2000).
keywords: Demonstration of Problems of Algebra Khayyam
Difficulties of the Postulates of Euclid Book

entries.label: The Jalali calendar and the Isfahan observatory
entries.hint: In 1074 Malik-Shah, on the advice of Nizam al-Mulk, set up an observatory at Isfahan under Omar Khayyam and others to reform the calendar; the Jalali calendar, adopted in 1079 and based on a solar year of 365.2424 days (as accurate as the later Gregorian reform), did not last under his successors but was the base of the Persian calendar of 1925.
entries.note: Omar Khayyam; Ibn al-Athir; Hillenbrand 1994; Edward Kennedy, ‘Omar Khayyam’, Mathematics Teacher (1975).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The tax assignments, the trade routes, the sack of Nishapur and the coinage

entries.label: The rural order and the Turkmen
entries.hint: The Turkmen who came with the Seljuks pastured their flocks on the highlands of Azerbaijan, Jibal and Khurasan and were an uneasy military force, which Nizam al-Mulk's regime tried to settle and control by allotting them iqtas and pastures; the peasants' obligations to the emirs and the poll and land taxes were set by the vizier's registers, and the tension between the herders and farmers was a theme of the Siyasatnama.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; Lambton 1988; Claude Cahen, Pre-Ottoman Turkey (1968).

entries.label: The trade of the Seljuk lands
entries.hint: The Seljuk peace helped the caravan trade across Iran: the textiles and ceramics of Rayy, Nishapur's lustre and the turquoise of its hills, the silk and the cotton of Khurasan, the horses of Turkistan and the slaves of the steppe were traded through Merv, Nishapur and Baghdad to Syria and Egypt; the minaret ribats and caravanserais on the roads (as at Ribat-i Sharaf) were built by the sultans and viziers.
entries.note: Richard Bulliet, Cotton, Climate, and Camels (2009); Hillenbrand 1994; Lambton 1988.

entries.label: The destruction of Nishapur and Merv
entries.hint: The Ghuzz sack of the great cities of Khurasan in 1153–1157, with their libraries, madrasas and the Nishapur observatory, killed thousands, depopulated the oasis of Merv, the largest city of the east, and began the long decline of Khurasan, which the Mongols completed in 1221; geographers like Yaqut, who saw Merv in 1220, still described rich libraries.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani; Yaqut, Mu'jam al-buldan; Bosworth 1968.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Isfahan observatory, the Jalali calendar and the caravanserais

entries.label: The Seljuk caravanserai and ribat
entries.hint: The Seljuks built or restored caravanserais at day's distance along the roads, with fortified courts, inner halls and iwans, the earlier examples being Ribat-i Malik (1068–1080, built by the Qarakhanid Shams al-Mulk) and Ribat-i Sharaf (1114–1115) in Khurasan; the type spread to Rum and became the standard of Anatolia's later caravanserais.
entries.note: Hillenbrand 1994; Kurt Erdmann, Das anatolische Karavansaray des 13. Jahrhunderts (1961); Bosworth 1968.

entries.label: The astronomical instruments of the Isfahan school
entries.hint: The Isfahan observatory's astronomers used the mural quadrant and the armillary sphere and in the following decades Muzaffar al-Isfizari and Abd al-Rahman al-Khazini of Merv, who compiled in 1115 the Sanjari Tables and a book on balances, with a hydrostatic balance for weighing metals and gems, continued the work in the Seljuk realm.
entries.note: Al-Khazini, Kitab mizan al-hikma; Kennedy 1975; Robert Hall, ‘al-Khazini’, Dictionary of Scientific Biography.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Byzantium, the Fatimids, the crusaders, Georgia, the Qarakhanids and the Kara-Khitai

entries.label: The Fatimids and the Seljuks
entries.hint: The Seljuks regarded the Fatimids as heretics and rivals, and conflicts on the Syrian frontier ran through the 1070s; the Fatimid vizier Badr al-Jamali (1073–1094) restored order in Egypt and held the coast, and after Tutush's death in 1095 the Fatimids recovered Jerusalem and Tyre in 1098 from the Artuqids, only to lose the city to the crusaders.
entries.note: Ibn al-Qalanisi; Ibn al-Athir; Hillenbrand 1999; Michael Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017).

entries.label: The Seljuks and the Byzantine succession
entries.hint: After Manzikert Alp Arslan made a treaty with Romanos and a fifty-year peace was agreed; the Seljuk prince Suleyman ibn Qutalmish, who had taken a base in Anatolia in 1075, was invited by the Byzantine claimant Nikephoros Melissenos and took Nicaea in 1081, founding the sultanate of Rum, which acknowledged Malik-Shah's overlordship; the diplomacy shows the empire's peripheral place for the central sultans.
entries.note: Attaleiates; Anna Komnene; Beihammer 2017; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The Qarakhanids and the Kara-Khitai
entries.hint: The Qarakhanid khans of Transoxiana, Muslim Turks, became vassals of Malik-Shah in 1089 and of Sanjar after 1102; in 1141 they were subordinated to the Kara-Khitai after Qatwan, and their dynasty was reduced to client rulers; the Seljuk relations with the Khwarazmshahs, who were their vassals and from 1156 successors, are in the same pattern.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Barthold, Turkestan down to the Mongol Invasion (1928); Biran 2005.

entries.label: Georgia and the battle of Didgori
entries.hint: David IV the Builder of Georgia, with Kipchak troops brought in by marriage and some 200 Frankish crusaders, defeated a Seljuk-Artuqid coalition army of several tens of thousands under Najm al-Din Ilghazi at Didgori in August 1121, and took Tbilisi in 1122; the victory made Georgia the leading Christian power in the Caucasus and ended the Seljuk claim to the region.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Ibn al-Azraq; Ibn al-Qalanisi; Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).
keywords: David IV the Builder of Georgia

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Turkmen migration, the earthquakes and the shift of the steppe frontier

entries.label: The Turkmen migration
entries.hint: Tens of thousands of Oghuz Turkmen families, with their sheep and horses, came from the Aral and Syr Darya steppes into Khurasan and moved west through northern Iran and Azerbaijan into Armenia, Anatolia and Syria, where the Seljuk state pushed them as a force against Byzantium; the movement, which changed the languages and people of western Asia, is the start of the Turkish settlement of Anatolia and Azerbaijan.
entries.note: Cahen 1968; Peter Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples (1992); Hillenbrand 2007.

entries.label: The earthquakes and famines of the age
entries.hint: A great earthquake in 1042 destroyed Tabriz and killed many thousands, and another in November 1114 struck northern Syria and south-eastern Anatolia, destroying Marash and Edessa's region; Ibn al-Athir and Michael the Syrian list these among many disasters of the age.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Nicholas Ambraseys and Charles Melville, A History of Persian Earthquakes (1982).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Terken Khatun, the slave soldiers, the viziers' families and the dervishes

entries.label: The Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians
entries.hint: The Jewish communities of Baghdad and Isfahan, and Christians of the Church of the East under the catholicos in Baghdad, the Jacobites and the Armenians in the north, lived under protected status; the Siyasatnama complains of Christians and Jews as officials, and the Zoroastrian communities of Fars and Yazd had fire temples and priests that survived, as shown by the Geniza letters and the Syriac chronicle of Michael the Syrian.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; Michael the Syrian, Chronicle; Cahen 1968; Mark Cohen, Under Crescent and Cross (1994).
keywords: Christians of the Church of the East

entries.label: The slave soldiers and ghulams
entries.hint: The sultans' slave soldiers (ghulams), bought on the steppes and raised in the court and given training, were the core of the standing army alongside the Turkmen levies and iqta holders; Nizam al-Mulk recommended a mixed force of Turks, Daylamites, Georgians and Arabs to avoid dependence, and they gave rise to the atabeg states.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama 30; Lambton 1988; David Ayalon.

entries.label: The viziers' families and the officials
entries.hint: Nizam al-Mulk's twelve sons and many relatives held the posts of vizier, governor and army commander, and the Nizamiyya family provided half of the Seljuk officials for decades; the rival families of Sharaf al-Mulk and Taj al-Mulk, the competition over the diwans, and the fall of vizier dynasties were a feature of the court.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Rawandi; Lambton 1988; Yavari 2014.

entries.label: Terken Khatun and the women of the court
entries.hint: Terken Khatun, the Qarakhanid wife of Malik-Shah and mother of Mahmud, who ruled with Taj al-Mulk after her husband's death in 1092, appointed officials and fought for her son's succession; Zubayda Khatun, mother of Barkyaruq, and Malik-Shah's daughter Mah-i Mulk Khatun, wife of the caliph al-Muqtadi, were powerful in the politics of the time, and the Seljuk women of the ruling class held property and built madrasas and tombs.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Rawandi; Lambton 1988; Hillenbrand 1994.
